properties.decision:
SETTLED (b) ON ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-16. REALIZES gains `conformance: unchecked | reviewed | verified`, DEFAULTING TO `unchecked`. A matching checksum keeps meaning only "the file has not moved"; whether anyone confirmed the file still does what the Requirement says becomes a thing the graph states rather than a thing a reader must remember to doubt.

THE DELIVERABLE IS THE COUNT, not the ceremony. "412 of 460 realizing edges were never checked against their requirement" is a sentence this design cannot say today, and it is what the property is for. A computation must READ it (`dec:edge-orthogonality`), so the property ships with the report that reads it or it does not ship.

(d) — raising it as a gap — is DEFERRED, not rejected, and becomes cheap once the data exists.
properties.name: A REALIZES edge says whether anyone checked the file against the rule — and `unchecked` is the default, so the silence becomes countable
properties.rationale:
THE EVIDENCE CAME FROM OUTSIDE, WHICH IS WHY IT COUNTS. A Requirement said the calendar day is the person's CIVIL date, not UTC. The realizing check-in used the ISO date of `createdAt`, which is UTC. The Capability said `realized`. The artifact's checksum matched its baseline, so `reconcile_artifacts` was silent. EVERY SIGNAL IN THE GRAPH WAS GREEN AND THE CODE DID NOT DO WHAT THE REQUIREMENT SAID — and THE USER FOUND IT IN THE PRODUCT. Alex's Grok session, 2026-08-14, item 5, judged the deepest of its fourteen.

THE SHAPE: REALIZES carries `completeness` and the Artifact carries a checksum. Between them they answer whether the file has MOVED since we looked. They do not answer, and cannot, whether it still IMPLEMENTS the property the Requirement states. Nothing distinguishes A FILE THAT WAS CHECKED AGAINST THE RULE from A FILE THAT WAS MERELY HASHED, and the two produce identical reports.

WHY THIS IS NOT A DETECTOR: reflow2 reads a DESIGN, never a running system, and judging whether code implements a civil-date rule is program analysis it deliberately stays out of (`dec:agent-navigates-content` keeps it out of file IO entirely). So every candidate was about RECORDING what is known, never computing it.

⭐ WHY (b) BEAT (a) — document the hole — AND THIS IS THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, not a preference: A DOCUMENTED HOLE IS SOMETHING A READER MUST REMEMBER; A DEFAULT OF `unchecked` IS SOMETHING THE GRAPH SAYS OUT LOUD, EVERY TIME, WITH NOBODY REMEMBERING ANYTHING. That is the same move made twice already this month and both times it was right: #200 stopped INJECTING a default nobody chose, and #213 started REPORTING the property nobody declared. Make the absence visible rather than implied.

WHY (c) LOST — lean on a Verification that names the PROPERTY rather than the file. Killed by its own evidence: HIS SESSION HAD A PASSING UNIT VERIFICATION AND SHIPPED THE BUG ANYWAY. A check that does not say what it covers changes nothing.

WHY (d) IS DEFERRED RATHER THAN REJECTED — surface it in the gap list. It is the strongest answer eventually and the wrong one FIRST: every REALIZES edge starts at `unchecked`, so a gap per edge is instant noise on a large design — and noise is exactly the failure just fixed in `loop_status` by `req:the-loop-can-say-what-this-session-owes`. Build (b) now; (d) costs almost nothing afterwards because the data will already be there.

⚠️ THE HONEST LIMIT OF (b), recorded so nobody later mistakes it for a guarantee: its value depends on people actually moving edges OFF `unchecked`, and NOTHING FORCES THAT. It may simply relocate the silence. What it does do unconditionally is make the silence COUNTABLE, and a number is something the loop can report and a person can act on where a documented caveat is not.

RELATED AND NOT REOPENED: `req:completion-computed` (delivery is computed from the thread, never asserted) and `cap:independent-evidence`. The tension this decision resolves is that completion is computed from EDGES, and an edge asserting realization was exactly the thing nobody checked.

ALSO WEIGHED: the same session marked two Capabilities `realized` on unit tests before a user had clicked through, and named that as its own error. `realized` vs `verified` ALREADY EXISTS in the capability lifecycle — so part of this was a missing PROMPT rather than a missing concept, which is why (a) was a genuine contender rather than a straw man.
